patches.old: Choice C is incorrect because surface molecules actually have slightly lower kinetic energy on average; evaporation preferentially removes the highest-energy surface molecules.
patches.new: Choice C is incorrect because kinetic energy is not what distinguishes the surface: a liquid at thermal equilibrium has the same mean molecular kinetic energy everywhere, since that is what its temperature measures. What differs at the surface is *potential* energy — a surface molecule has fewer attractive neighbours, so it sits higher in energy, and that energy cost per unit area is exactly what γ measures.
patches.reason: The published explanation claimed surface molecules have lower average kinetic energy. At equilibrium the mean kinetic energy is uniform throughout the liquid — it is the definition of temperature — and the asymmetry that creates surface tension is in potential energy, not kinetic. (Evaporative cooling removes the fastest molecules, but that is a non-equilibrium process and does not make the surface permanently colder.) The corrected version also connects the asymmetry directly to γ as energy per unit area, which is how the lesson defines it.

patches.old: A common mistake is to think the area (proportional to r^2) is the relevant factor, which would predict a fourfold increase, but the geometry of the meniscus depends on the radius linearly.
patches.new: The reason for the inverse dependence is worth seeing: surface tension pulls along the contact line, whose length is the perimeter 2πr, while the weight it must hold up is that of a column of cross-section πr². Setting γ(2πr)cosθ = ρgh(πr²) leaves one factor of r in the denominator, so h ∝ 1/r. A common mistake is to use the area (∝ r²) and predict a fourfold increase.
patches.reason: The published note dismissed the r² error by asserting that 'the geometry of the meniscus depends on the radius linearly', which explains nothing. The actual reason — force scales with the perimeter while weight scales with the area, leaving one net factor of r — is the derivation the lesson already gives a few sections earlier, and it is what makes the 1/r relationship memorable.

visual.title: The surface, the sphere, and the narrow tube
visual.alt: A molecular picture contrasting a bulk molecule pulled evenly in all directions with a surface molecule pulled only inward; two alveoli joined by an airway, the smaller at higher pressure emptying into the larger, with a note that surfactant lowers surface tension more as an alveolus shrinks; capillary rise higher in a narrow tube than a wide one, with mercury sitting lower inside its tube; and a table of surface tension values with the Laplace equations.
visual.caption: A molecule at the surface is missing half its neighbours, and γ is the energy price of that. The same γ then sets two things the MCAT asks about constantly: the pressure inside a small sphere, 2γ/R, and how high a liquid climbs a narrow tube, 2γcosθ/ρgr.
